wave-platform.title: Wave Platform
wave-platform.tagline: One marketing-automation SaaS — the product, the platform it runs on and an internal financial system.
wave-platform.summary: Senior engineer at Group Wave Enterprise, owning both product and platform: 1,000+ merged PRs in six months across infrastructure, backend and frontend.
wave-platform.role: Senior Software Engineer · product & platform owner
wave-platform.overview: Group Wave Enterprise builds marketing-automation products. I joined to work across the whole stack — NestJS backend, React frontend and the infrastructure underneath — while the platform was being redesigned, and ended up owning three areas: the platform itself, the campaign-automation engine and an internal financial system.
wave-platform.problem: The product had grown as a set of microservices that were expensive to evolve and operate for the size of the team. Some workflows were slow, CPU-heavy work competed with request handling, builds shared resources with production, and there were no shared standards for repositories, pipelines, testing or observability.
wave-platform.approach: Together with an external software-architecture consultant I helped define the new platform architecture and contributed to the migration to a modular React/NestJS monolith. In parallel I took ownership of the platform — Kubernetes, CI/CD, databases, observability and security — and built the product areas described below, each change small and documented (decisions as ADRs, operations as runbooks).
wave-platform.architecture: Simplified view. The NestJS monolith pushes heavy work to workers — one deployment per queue, scaled on queue depth by KEDA — and reaches PostgreSQL through PgBouncer. Redis, RabbitMQ and MinIO run next to it on Kubernetes; Jenkins builds and deploys; OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana and Loki observe everything.
challenges: Migrating from microservices to a modular monolith while product features kept shipping.
Separating CPU-bound jobs from request handling without duplicating work — solved with per-queue workers, autoscaling and BullMQ job deduplication.
Keeping database connections under control as the number of workers grew.
Building a financial system where a security mistake is expensive, without slowing the finance team down.
outcomes: Application workflows more than 70% faster through refactoring, caching, BullMQ job deduplication and dedicated workers.
1,000+ merged pull requests in about six months across infrastructure, backend and frontend.
Backend PR pipeline 26% faster and a ~41% smaller backend image.
CI isolated from production, faster feedback on PRs and every pipeline change documented as an ADR.
Observability with SLOs and alerts that are tied to runbooks and post-mortems.
An internal financial platform in daily use, plus a campaign-automation engine and an external API.
A shared Claude Code RAG knowledge base and reusable LLM skills/agents for the engineering team.
lessons: A modular monolith gives a small team most of the isolation of microservices with a fraction of the operational cost.
Platform engineering pays off fastest when it is encoded in templates and pipelines, not in documents.
Writing each decision down as an ADR is what made it possible to change CI three times without losing the reasoning.
wave-platform.note: Internal and client details are confidential. This case study stays at the level of my résumé: no vendors, internal names or security specifics.

chapters.title: Platform & reliability
chapters.body: Most of my work happened below the product: making the platform cheaper to run, safer to change and observable.
points: CI/CD rebuilt in three phases — GitHub Actions → self-hosted ephemeral runners on Kubernetes → standalone Jenkins provisioned with Ansible and configured as code — with CI isolated from production, priority per branch and only the affected tests (with diff coverage) on pull requests. Profiling cut backend PR time by 26% (lint + tests 380 s → 244 s), the backend image by ~41% (2.5 GB → 1.5 GB) and one build step from ~285 s to ~5 s.
Workers split into one deployment per queue, each with its own resources and connection budget, autoscaled on queue depth with KEDA.

A PostgreSQL connection-management project: PgBouncer, per-worker connection budgets, cleanup of idle transactions and memory tuning — plus automated, encrypted off-site backups and audited, least-privilege database access for engineers.

Observability end to end: OpenTelemetry traces correlated with logs (and a copyable trace ID in the UI), Prometheus with Thanos, Loki, Grafana dashboards, Grafana Faro for real-user monitoring, SLOs with multi-window burn-rate alerts, runbooks and post-mortems.
Security baseline: secrets out of the repositories, secret scanning and static analysis in CI and pre-commit, SSO for internal tools and a hardened ingress.

Incident response and audits: root-cause analysis of production incidents (table bloat, disk I/O saturation — including a query-logging loop growing ~20 GB/h that competed with the database's write-ahead log — and a runaway budget automation), each turned into fixes, guardrails and alerts; plus a multi-tenant readiness audit with a GO/NO-GO assessment and a phased 13-sprint plan.

chapters.title: Campaign automation engine
chapters.body: Media buyers describe rules — when a campaign's metrics cross a threshold, change its budget or status — and the platform runs them on a schedule.
points: A rules engine with conditions on sales, spend and checkout data, budget and status actions, time-window scheduling and manual or automatic target selection.
Execution runs on dedicated workers; every run records the rule version in force, what happened to each target and why nothing happened when a rule was skipped.
A versioned external API with per-tenant keys, rate limiting and a published OpenAPI contract, so other systems can read the same data.

chapters.title: Internal financial platform
chapters.body: An internal system that replaced spreadsheets for the group's finance team. I led its design and built most of it, backend and frontend. Security details are deliberately kept general here.
points: Ledger and ERP: bank and card-account sync through queues with per-account progress, multi-currency P&L at daily exchange rates, CSV import and export, and automatic matching of internal transfers.
A categorization rules engine where the most specific rule wins and conflicts are shown before saving, plus bulk categorization and suggestions.
Finance operations: commissions with monthly close snapshots, contractor payroll, invoices, tax forecasting, performance bonuses, accounting documents, a partner registry and an activities suite.

Defense in depth: tenant isolation enforced by the database as well as the application, encrypted and masked sensitive data with audited access, a tamper-evident audit trail, step-up authentication for critical actions, time-bound access with reports and alerts, and security checks in CI.

rickos.title: RickOS
rickos.tagline: A local-first personal operating system with an AI layer built on Claude Code.
rickos.summary: What started as a time tracker became a desktop + mobile command centre for time, tasks, habits, learning, finances and projects — with AI features that run the local Claude Code CLI.
rickos.overview: RickOS is the tool I use to run my own days. It began as a simple working-time tracker and grew, one module at a time, into a single panel: a timeline time tracker with Pomodoro, inbox/TODO/habits, a Learning OS (roadmaps, Markdown notes, AI-generated flashcards with SM-2 spaced repetition, quizzes and Obsidian export), finances, a flight-price monitor, GitHub-synced projects and a worktree health scanner.
rickos.problem: My work, study and personal planning lived in a dozen apps that didn't talk to each other, and none of them could use the AI tooling I already rely on every day.
rickos.approach: A headless Fastify server is the only owner of the database and exposes everything through a single RPC endpoint plus server-sent events. The Electron app and a PWA I use on my phone are just clients of that server. AI features shell out to the local Claude Code CLI, stream results live and can run in the background.
rickos.architecture: Both clients talk to one Fastify server over RPC + SSE. SQLite runs in WebAssembly (sql.js) with versioned migrations; secrets are encrypted with AES-256-GCM; remote access requires a token.

chapters.title: AI layer
points: Prompt Runner: parallel tabs that combine an agent, a set of skills, a project and a prompt, run through the local Claude Code CLI with live streaming.
Brain dump: free text in, tasks, projects and calendar entries out.
AI-generated flashcards and quizzes in the Learning OS, and a daily briefing on the dashboard.
Token usage of every AI run is recorded per module and per project.

chapters.title: Modules
points: Time tracker: a continuous 24-hour timeline with draggable blocks, tags, Pomodoro, a monthly heatmap and an hour bank.
Organisation: inbox with a global capture shortcut, TODO with priorities and due dates, habits with monthly grids and insights, weekly review and a knowledge base.
Projects: GitHub issues on a Kanban board, and a scanner that flags local branches and worktrees that are at risk, forgotten, orphaned or safe to clean.
Finances, travel (flight-price monitoring) and links, all optional and configurable.

chapters.title: Engineering
points: One RPC registry shared by the desktop and the web: the same handlers serve Electron and the phone.
A Playwright script captures every page at desktop and phone sizes in two visual skins, so UI changes are reviewed side by side.
Daily database snapshots and a one-file export and import.

challenges: Keeping one source of truth while serving a desktop app and a phone at the same time.
Running long AI jobs (prompt runner, brain dump → tasks, flashcard generation) without blocking the UI.
Integrating GitHub, multi-account Google Calendar OAuth, Pluggy Open Finance and Skyscanner behind one consistent interface.
outcomes: Daily-driver tool with 170+ commits and counting.
Runs as a desktop app and as an installable PWA from the same server and database.
Automated Playwright screenshot suite that captures every page at desktop and phone sizes in two skins.
lessons: Local-first plus a thin server is a surprisingly powerful architecture for personal software.
Treating an AI CLI as a subprocess you orchestrate is more flexible than embedding a single API call.
rickos.note: Screenshots use a separate demo database filled with fictional data.

telecom-subscriptions.title: Telecom Subscription Platform
telecom-subscriptions.tagline: Serverless subscription management for the largest telecom company in Argentina.
telecom-subscriptions.summary: Backend engineer at Agile Content on a high-volume subscription platform: purchase, billing, renewal and cancellation services on AWS, handling millions of events per month.
telecom-subscriptions.overview: At Agile Content I worked on the subscription-management platform behind the digital products of the biggest telecom company in Argentina. The platform runs critical, money-moving flows: purchase, billing, renewal and cancellation.
telecom-subscriptions.problem: High-volume transactional services must be reliable, observable and cheap to operate, and every change has to be safe to deploy.
telecom-subscriptions.approach: I developed and maintained microservices — Node.js APIs and serverless functions — took part in defining architecture and project patterns, and created and maintained the infrastructure with Docker, Terraform, the Serverless Framework and CI/CD.
telecom-subscriptions.architecture: Simplified view. Node.js APIs and Lambda functions communicate through SQS, persist to RDS and S3, feed Redshift for analytics and are traced with CloudWatch and X-Ray.
challenges: Designing for high availability in services where every failure affects a customer's subscription.
Making a distributed, event-driven system observable end to end.
Raising test confidence across many small services.
outcomes: AWS-based solutions (Lambda, SQS, CloudWatch, ECS, X-Ray, Parameter Store, S3, Redshift, RDS) supporting millions of events per month.
Led internal API-testing libraries built on Robot Framework and reached 100% unit-test coverage, significantly improving deployment confidence.
Contributed to architecture decisions and service patterns that improved reliability and reduced incident frequency.
Built datasets and reports with Tableau and QuickSight.
lessons: In serverless systems, observability is part of the architecture, not an add-on.
Shared testing libraries scale quality better than per-service heroics.
telecom-subscriptions.note: Client systems are confidential; details are limited to what is on my public résumé.

ai-assistant-rag.title: AI Assistant Re-architecture
ai-assistant-rag.tagline: Redesigning an AI product around retrieval — and cutting its AI bill by more than 90%.
ai-assistant-rag.summary: Consulting project: replaced an expensive AI setup with a RAG pipeline on a vector database, fixed critical security issues in an AI-generated codebase and made the product configurable without developers.
ai-assistant-rag.overview: ErosAI's product included an AI assistant built quickly, largely with AI-generated code. It worked, but it was costly, limited in how much knowledge it could use, and had security and reliability problems.
ai-assistant-rag.problem: Monthly AI infrastructure costs were high, the knowledge base had size limits, responses were slow, and the codebase had unauthorized access to admin pages, sensitive-data exposure, Service Worker caching issues and inconsistent data from multiple sources of truth.
ai-assistant-rag.approach: I redesigned the AI architecture as a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline backed by a vector database, then refactored the application: modularised it, extracted reusable components, applied design patterns and replaced hard-coded values with an admin-configurable system. Finally I added monitoring and observability.
ai-assistant-rag.architecture: Simplified view. Knowledge is chunked and embedded into a vector database; each question retrieves only the most relevant context before calling the LLM.
challenges: Fixing security issues in a codebase nobody had fully designed.
Keeping answers good while sending far less context to the model.
Removing hard-coded configuration without breaking a live product.
outcomes: Monthly AI infrastructure costs reduced by over 90%.
Better response quality, no more knowledge-base size limit and significantly lower latency.
Critical security and reliability issues resolved.
Configuration changes no longer require a developer.
Detailed error tracking and faster root-cause analysis in production.
lessons: AI-generated code ships fast; architecture and security review is what makes it last.
Retrieval is usually cheaper and better than a bigger prompt.
ai-assistant-rag.note: Client details are confidential; figures come from my résumé.

public-security-platform.title: Public Security Intelligence Platform
public-security-platform.tagline: High-throughput integrations for a police intelligence platform used by government agencies.
public-security-platform.summary: At IPQ Tecnologia I helped develop and scale a public-security platform, building Kafka integrations that process more than 2 million messages a day.
public-security-platform.overview: IPQ Tecnologia builds a public-security and police-intelligence platform used by government agencies. I worked on integrations, map layers and confidential core operational modules.
public-security-platform.problem: Critical systems needed to exchange data in real time, in an environment with strict reliability and confidentiality requirements.
public-security-platform.approach: I architected and implemented high-throughput integrations on Kafka, built map layers and integrations between systems, and worked on core operational modules. I also worked on a CMS for registering electronic components, monitoring and an equipment map.
public-security-platform.architecture: Deliberately abstract. External and field systems publish to Kafka; Node.js integration services and Django modules consume, store and present the data on maps.
challenges: Sustaining millions of messages per day without losing data.
Working inside strict confidentiality constraints.
outcomes: Integrations processing more than 2 million messages per day.
Part of the team behind a platform associated with a reported crime reduction of over 30%.
lessons: Message-driven integration is what lets very different critical systems evolve independently.
public-security-platform.note: Confidential government system — no internal details are shown.

tindergpt.title: TinderGPT
tindergpt.tagline: An LLM that writes your openers — my most-starred open-source project and a NodeBR talk.
tindergpt.summary: Generates ChatGPT replies and openers for dating-app matches and sends them automatically, with pluggable AI providers and social platforms.
tindergpt.overview: TinderGPT started as a playful question — could an LLM keep a dating-app conversation going? — and became an open-source project with 22 stars and the subject of my talk at NodeBR #63 in São Paulo.
tindergpt.problem: Starting and sustaining conversations is repetitive. The technical question was how to build it so the AI provider and the platform could be swapped without rewriting the app.
tindergpt.approach: A TypeScript Express API uses factory patterns for both AI providers and social platforms, a dependency container and auth middleware, with Redis for auth storage. A React (Ant Design) dashboard controls targeting filters such as distance and bio. Everything runs with Docker Compose.
tindergpt.architecture: The API routes every action through two factories — one for social platforms, one for AI providers — so new integrations are additive.
challenges: Respecting the platform's rate limits (HTTP 429) with deliberate pacing.
Designing prompts that produce natural, context-aware messages.
outcomes: 22 GitHub stars — my most-starred repository.
Presented at NodeBR #63 (São Paulo, 2023).
lessons: Abstractions around LLM providers pay off immediately — the model landscape changes monthly.

mindsight-hr.title: Mindsight HR Platforms
mindsight-hr.tagline: Multi-tenant HR systems, enterprise SSO and a job board built end to end.
mindsight-hr.summary: Full-stack engineer on multi-tenant HR platforms used by tens of thousands of people a month: SSO with external IdPs, OAuth2 between services and a Django + React job board.
mindsight-hr.overview: Mindsight builds HR software for recruitment and hiring. I designed and delivered features, refactored legacy services and improved stability across multi-tenant platforms.
mindsight-hr.problem: Enterprise customers needed to sign in with their own identity providers, internal systems needed secure service-to-service communication, and some critical processing flows were too heavy.
mindsight-hr.approach: I developed authentication and system-communication features — SSO login with external IdPs, OAuth2 for internal communication and event journaling for compliance — and, in a team of two, built a job-board application end to end.
mindsight-hr.architecture: Simplified view. The Django platform authenticates users through external IdPs, talks to internal services over OAuth2 and records events in a journal.
challenges: Adding SSO to a multi-tenant system without breaking existing tenants.
Refactoring critical flows while they served real users.
outcomes: Critical processing flows refactored, reducing memory consumption and execution time by over 50%.
Job board delivered end to end with a key role in architecture, data modelling, API design, testing and deployment.
SSO, OAuth2 and event journaling supporting compliance.
lessons: In multi-tenant systems, authentication is product work, not plumbing.

trama-expedicoes.title: Trama de Expedições
trama-expedicoes.tagline: A 3D mobile squad game — client, match server and online services — built solo with AI agents.
trama-expedicoes.summary: Unity PvPvE squad game in active development: an authoritative match server for Linux, client-side prediction, matchmaking, accounts, clans, parties and an automated visual QA suite that captures every screen.
trama-expedicoes.overview: Trama de Expedições is a personal game project and an experiment in building something large with AI agents as collaborators. In about a month it went from a movement lab to online matches against a dedicated server, with a full set of menus, social features and a progression loop. It is honest about where it is: everything below is verified by automated scenarios, not yet by human playtests, and there is no validated mobile build.
trama-expedicoes.problem: Can one person, working with AI agents, build the technical foundations of a multiplayer mobile game — networking, online services, balancing, content pipeline and QA — to a professional standard?
trama-expedicoes.approach: A Unity client and a headless match server share one .NET core library, so the rules are identical on both sides. Online services (accounts, friends, clans, chat, parties, mail, ranking and economy) live in a separate .NET 8 service on PostgreSQL. Every change goes through an automated scenario runner and is documented for the agents: project state, a hand-off file, open items and nine ADRs.
trama-expedicoes.architecture: The Unity client talks to an authoritative match server over UDP and to the meta service for everything outside a match. The match server runs in Docker on Linux; a shared .NET core keeps rules identical on client and server; bots fill rooms and drive automated balancing runs.

chapters.title: Networking and matchmaking
points: Dedicated, authoritative match server built for Linux and packaged in Docker (88 MB image).
Client-side prediction for the player's own squad: p95 position error of 0.4–0.5 m at 200–300 ms of latency.
Tested on a grid of 16 network conditions: responses arrive at the round-trip time plus about 85–130 ms, and packet loss only costs smoothness.
Rooms open on demand per game mode and close by themselves; a short queue fills empty seats with bots.
Parties: invite friends, ready up and join the same team; ranked play is solo only.

chapters.title: Online services
points: A .NET 8 service on PostgreSQL for accounts, friends, clans with chat, parties, mail, ranking and economy.
Recoverable login with an emailed code; Google and Apple sign-in are written but not yet wired to real keys.
The match server checks every party key with the service, so a client cannot fake one.

chapters.title: Automated visual QA
points: A scenario runner drives the real game build and captures 31 screens at four aspect ratios, plus empty, loading, error and long-name states.
Screens are scored against the design mock-ups (SSIM with the 3D background masked) and checked by eye before and after each change.
A review of 242 visual issues became ten stacked pull requests, each with its own scenarios passing.

chapters.title: Art pipeline
points: A "toy board" art standard documented in an ADR: calm ground, chunky pieces, only gameplay draws attention.
Map kits modelled by code in Blender with Python; the whole map is 341k triangles, against 1.78M for one quadrant of the previous version.
Measurable readability criteria checked by a script on every capture.

challenges: Keeping game rules deterministic between client and server.
Making latency and packet loss invisible on a mobile-style game without a real network test yet.
Balancing maps without a player base.
Keeping dozens of UI screens consistent across aspect ratios and edge cases.
outcomes: 600+ commits and 190+ merged pull requests, most of them from AI-agent branches.
72 bot matches per map kept each of 6 maps between 35% and 65% win rate.
Stress test with 400 units at a p95 frame time of about 3.3–3.5 ms (headless, Mac).
Skeletal animation with LOD for 18 characters.
lessons: AI agents are productive when the project's state and decisions are written down for them.
Automated screenshots plus a human review loop scale far better than manual QA for UI.
trama-expedicoes.note: Source is private while the game is in development. Screenshots come from the automated test runs of the development build.

smoketrack.title: SmokeTrack
smoketrack.tagline: A private, offline quantified-self app to understand — and quit — smoking.
smoketrack.summary: Log every cigarette with context and mood, then see patterns: moving averages, hour × day heatmaps, intervals, longest gaps, triggers and period comparisons. Runs as a PWA and as an iOS app.
smoketrack.overview: SmokeTrack is a small product with a personal purpose: help people (me first) notice the patterns behind their smoking. Everything stays on the device — no account, no backend.
smoketrack.problem: Quitting apps either nag or demand accounts. I wanted something private that turns a simple log into insight.
smoketrack.approach: React + TypeScript + Vite with Tailwind, local-first storage, Recharts for analysis and a PWA plus a Capacitor iOS build. Additive JSON import/export with validation and data migration keeps data portable as the model evolves.

chapters.title: What the analysis shows
points: Daily, weekday and weekend averages, and a daily chart with a 7-day moving average.
Intervals between records (mean, median, p90) and the longest gap without smoking.
An hour × weekday heatmap and the most frequent triggers (activity × time of day) compared with the average.
Breakdowns by activity, type and mood, plus a comparison with the previous period.
A 365-day consumption calendar and a per-day timeline that ignore the filters.
Filters by period or calendar month, weekdays or weekends, totals or daily averages.

challenges: Making analysis useful with only a few data points a day.
Evolving the data model safely on users' devices.
outcomes: Shipped as a PWA on GitHub Pages and packaged for iOS with Capacitor.
Record editing, mood and notes added without breaking existing data, thanks to the migration layer.
Analytics covered by Vitest unit tests.
lessons: Privacy is a feature: no account means no friction to start.

clanmanager.title: ClanManager
clanmanager.tagline: A serverless war dashboard for a Clash of Clans clan.
clanmanager.summary: A scheduled AWS Lambda pulls clan-war data from the official game API into DynamoDB, and a React dashboard ranks every member.
clanmanager.overview: Built for my own clan: who attacked, how much destruction, who missed attacks — across normal and league wars.
clanmanager.problem: The game shows wars one at a time; leaders need history to decide who plays.
clanmanager.approach: A Serverless Framework Lambda runs every 23 hours, executes different workflows for league wars and normal wars, and stores results through a data-service factory that can switch between DynamoDB and local storage. Custom error types handle cases like a war in progress or API maintenance.
clanmanager.architecture: A scheduled Lambda extracts data from the official API and writes to DynamoDB; the React dashboard reads the aggregated results.
outcomes: Live dashboard used by the clan.
lessons: Serverless + a schedule is the cheapest possible way to run a data pipeline for a community.

squadbusters-tournaments.title: Squad Busters Community Hub
squadbusters-tournaments.tagline: Tournaments, records and leaderboards for a game community — plus a Discord bot.
squadbusters-tournaments.summary: Django + DRF platform with tournaments, clan records and leaderboards fed by external game APIs, and a discord.js bot that answers player-stat queries.
squadbusters-tournaments.overview: A community platform for Squad Busters players with separate Django apps for core, records, leaderboard and integrations.
squadbusters-tournaments.approach: Integration services model players, heroes and units across nine migrations; a Discord bot calls the site's API and replies with sorted totals.
outcomes: Platform and bot built and run for a player community.

cimatec-industrial.title: Industrial Systems at SENAI CIMATEC
cimatec-industrial.tagline: Greenhouse automation, fleet management and wind-tower traceability for startups.
cimatec-industrial.summary: As an intern I worked on three outsourced systems: greenhouse sensor monitoring, a vehicle fleet and reservation API I designed, and traceability for wind-tower manufacturing parts.
cimatec-industrial.overview: SENAI CIMATEC develops systems for startups and industry. Over a year I worked on three of them.
cimatec-industrial.approach: I owned, under supervision, the architecture and development of a fleet-management and reservation API, collaborated on a greenhouse monitoring and automation system, and on a traceability system for wind-tower parts that tracks parts through manufacturing and reports what is needed to complete a tower.
outcomes: Fleet API optimised logistics and resource allocation.
Traceability software enabled seamless tracking of parts and supported a large increase in production output.

woo-nomad-woo.title: Woo Nomad Woo
woo-nomad-woo.tagline: A social network for digital nomads — my Computer Science capstone.
woo-nomad-woo.summary: Cities, countries, reviews, ratings and articles for nomads, with an Express + Prisma API, a React web app and an Expo mobile app.
woo-nomad-woo.overview: A palindrome name for a platform about travelling and coming back: nomads rate and review cities, share recommendations and write articles.
woo-nomad-woo.approach: Express with Prisma and SQLite (migrations and seeds), a React + Vite + Tailwind + Redux Toolkit web app with Firebase, and an Expo / React Native mobile client.
outcomes: Presented as my Computer Science final project.

mba-thesis.title: Serverless × Microservices (MBA research)
mba-thesis.tagline: MBA thesis: integrating serverless computing with a microservices architecture.
mba-thesis.summary: Research and experiments for my USP MBA thesis — cold starts, tracing and state with Lambda, X-Ray, CloudWatch, DynamoDB and SQS, using an AI chat-bot simulation as the workload.
mba-thesis.overview: My MBA in Software Engineering at USP ended with a thesis on integrating serverless computing with microservices architecture.
mba-thesis.approach: Python Lambdas (an AI bot simulation using ChatGPT or Gemini behind a provider factory, and a notification service) work alongside Node.js chat-management services in Docker Compose. Latency-test scripts measure the effects of cold starts and the hybrid design.
outcomes: Thesis completed; MBA concluded with a final grade of 8.5.

punk-records.title: Punk Records
punk-records.tagline: A knowledge-centric platform where entities own knowledge and agents are disposable.
punk-records.summary: Experiment in multi-agent systems: knowledge stored as Markdown + Git, AI output through a staging → review pipeline, and a CEO-agent orchestrating specialist agents.
punk-records.overview: Two iterations. v1 is a Python monorepo (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy + Alembic, embeddings, a Next.js web app, Postgres in Docker) with replaceable agent runtimes. v2, the "startup factory", uses a containerised agent engine as executor and Punk Records as the knowledge layer, with local models via Ollama and a Telegram interface.
outcomes: Working prototypes of both iterations.
lessons: Agents are cheap; curated knowledge is the asset.
punk-records.note: Private repository. Third-party projects vendored in the repo are not my work and are not shown.

republica-dos-bilhoes.title: República dos Bilhões
republica-dos-bilhoes.tagline: A satirical Brazilian tycoon roguelite for mobile.
republica-dos-bilhoes.summary: Godot 4 prototype: start with R$100k and build an empire through decision cards, influence, risk and crises — with balancing simulations and fully data-driven content.
republica-dos-bilhoes.overview: A portrait, tap-only mobile game. About 100 events, contacts, news templates and empire tables are pure JSON content packs; no real people or companies are named.
republica-dos-bilhoes.approach: Save/restore preserves the random-number state; unit tests, headless UI smoke tests and a balancing simulation (4 bots × 300 runs) run from a Makefile. The build followed a documented 8-prompt plan with AI agents.
outcomes: Playable prototype with automated balancing.

campus-party-serverless.title: Serverless API in an hour
campus-party-serverless.tagline: Live-coding demo for my Campus Party workshop on AWS.
campus-party-serverless.summary: Lambda handlers behind API Gateway with DynamoDB, plus a React to-do client — the code I built live with the audience.
campus-party-serverless.overview: Companion code for the workshop "Building a serverless API on AWS" at Campus Party (2023).
outcomes: Workshop delivered at Campus Party's Supernova workshop arena.

hololens-city.title: HoloLens City
hololens-city.tagline: A mixed-reality city you place on a table — for Campus Party 2018.
hololens-city.summary: Air-tap to place a 3D city; highlighted buildings open panels about tourism, rentals, restaurants, events and news.
hololens-city.overview: Built at SENAI CIMATEC with Unity, C# and HoloToolkit as one of the HoloLens projects we took to Campus Party 2018.
outcomes: Demo built for Campus Party 2018.

travel-buddy-finder.title: Travel Buddy Finder
travel-buddy-finder.tagline: Learning project: microservices for a digital-nomad social network.
travel-buddy-finder.summary: A Serverless AI-bot Lambda (ChatGPT and Gemini behind a provider factory), shared TypeScript packages and a Django locations service — with most of the product still on the drawing board.
travel-buddy-finder.overview: A deliberately over-architected sandbox to practise microservices around a product I care about. Notification and bot workflows are designed and diagrammed; only part is implemented.

event-driven-studies.title: Event-driven studies
event-driven-studies.tagline: Kafka chat and a NestJS + RabbitMQ service — small systems to learn messaging properly.
event-driven-studies.summary: A real-time chat on Express, Socket.IO and KafkaJS, and a NestJS service with MongoDB image storage, RabbitMQ and an email worker.

compilers.title: Compiler front-end
compilers.tagline: From Wirth notation to automata, lexical and syntactic analysis.
compilers.summary: University project in Python: builds an automaton from simplified Wirth notation, removes empty, non-deterministic, inaccessible and equivalent transitions, then performs lexical and partial syntactic analysis.

greendotsys.title: GreenDotSys
greendotsys.tagline: Energy monitoring and CO₂ awareness for hotels.
greendotsys.summary: Team project: reads room energy sensors, alerts when energy is used while guests are away and estimates avoided CO₂, with a sensor simulator.

gameducation-hackathon.title: Gameducation
gameducation-hackathon.tagline: Hackathon prototype — course recommendations and a motivation bot for students.
gameducation-hackathon.summary: Built in a weekend at Hacking.Rio 2021: a profile survey that recommends courses, a bot that follows progress and a gamified dashboard.

legends-of-senai.title: Legends of SENAI
legends-of-senai.tagline: A turn-based strategy game built by five students.
legends-of-senai.summary: C# / UWP game with characters, skills, a battle map and a world map, built for a programming-languages course.

aleatory-scripts.title: Aleatory scripts
aleatory-scripts.tagline: A drawer of small tools and automations.
aleatory-scripts.summary: Scripts written to test, study or automate: a Three.js secret-Santa draw, a Vigenère cipher break, game calculators, exporters and more.

selltime.title: SellTime
selltime.tagline: Early startup attempt — a cross-platform app.
selltime.summary: Xamarin.Forms app prototype for a startup idea. Story to be written.
